subsection: 1. Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms

notes.h: Ireland's Ice Age and types of ice
notes.b: Ireland was glaciated during the Pleistocene, and the landforms in this subsection were shaped by ice in its two main cold stages.
points: The older cold stage is the Munsterian; the more recent is the Midlandian.
Munsterian ice covered almost all of the island.
Midlandian glaciation ended about 10,000 years ago, and its ice did not cover the far south of Ireland.
An ice sheet is a continental mass of ice covering whole landscapes, as in Antarctica and Greenland today.
A valley glacier is confined to a valley and is fed by snow and ice from corries on the mountainside.
Snow that survives the summer is compacted into firn (granular snow, also called nevé).
Firn becomes glacier ice as the weight of overlying snow squeezes out the air and the ice crystals grow larger and interlock.

notes.b: A glacier gains ice at its head and loses it at its snout, and the balance between these determines its behaviour.
points: Accumulation zone: the upper part of the glacier, where snow and ice are gained.
Ablation zone: the lower part, including the snout, where ice is lost by melting.
Equilibrium line: the boundary between the two zones, where gain and loss are equal over a year.
Basal slip: meltwater at the base lubricates the bed, so the whole glacier slides over the rock.
Internal deformation (plastic flow): ice crystals slip past one another under the weight of the ice, so the glacier flows downhill.
Rotational movement: ice in a corrie rotates within the hollow instead of moving straight down the valley.
Ice moves fastest at the centre of the surface and slowest at the sides and base, where friction with the valley walls and bed is greatest.

notes.h: Advance and retreat of the snout
notes.b: The snout's position depends on whether more ice arrives from the accumulation zone than melts at the snout.
points: Advance: when more ice arrives from the accumulation zone than melts, the snout moves forward.
Retreat: when melting exceeds the ice arriving, the snout moves back up the valley, although the ice is still flowing forward.
Heavier snowfall or cooler summers, which reduce melting, cause the glacier to advance.
Less snowfall or warmer summers, which increase melting, cause the glacier to retreat.

notes.b: Average rate of movement is found by dividing the distance moved by the number of years. The figures below are illustrative, invented for practice.
points: Average rate = distance moved ÷ number of years, given in metres per year.
Illustrative: a snout that retreats 600 m over 20 years has moved an average of 600 ÷ 20 = 30 m per year.
Illustrative: a snout that advances 450 m over 9 years has moved an average of 450 ÷ 9 = 50 m per year.

notes.b: Glaciers erode mainly by plucking and abrasion, while freeze-thaw supplies rock debris at the edges of the ice.
points: Plucking (quarrying): meltwater enters joints in the bedrock and freezes, bonding the ice to the rock; as the glacier moves on, it tears out blocks, mainly on the downhill side of rock obstacles.
Abrasion: rock fragments frozen into the base of the ice scrape and polish the bedrock.
Rock flour: fine powder ground from the bedrock by abrasion, which meltwater carries away, giving glacial lakes a milky colour.
Freeze-thaw on the rock above and beside the ice: water freezing in cracks breaks off fragments, which fall onto the ice and are carried away.
1. Snow collects in a hollow on the mountainside; nivation (erosion by snow patches) and freeze-thaw enlarge the hollow.
2. The snow turns to ice, and the rotating glacier plucks and abrades the back wall and floor, deepening the hollow and steepening the back wall.
3. The result is a bowl with a steep back wall and a rock lip, called the threshold, at its lower edge.
4. When the ice melts, water collects behind the lip and forms a lake called a tarn.
Examples: Coumshingaun, Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford; the Devil's Punchbowl, Mangerton, Co. Kerry.
Diagram: cross-section of a corrie with steep back wall, rock lip and tarn; plan view of the bowl-shaped hollow.

notes.h: Arête and pyramidal peak (erosion, upland stage)
points: 1. Two corries cut back into the mountainside from opposite sides of a ridge.
2. Their back walls retreat, sharpening the ridge between them into a thin, knife-edged arête.
3. Three or more corries erode back around one summit from different directions.
4. The summit is left as a sharp, pointed pyramidal peak, also called a horn.
Arête example: Striding Edge, Helvellyn, Lake District, England.
Pyramidal peak examples: Carrauntoohil, Macgillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry, Ireland's highest mountain; the Matterhorn, Swiss-Italian Alps.
Diagram: plan view of two corries backing onto an arête; plan view of a horn ringed by three corries.
1. Before glaciation the valley is V-shaped, cut by a river.
2. A glacier fills the valley and deepens and widens its floor by plucking and abrasion.
3. The glacier cuts off the river's interlocking spurs, leaving blunt cliff faces called truncated spurs.
4. The result is a broad, flat-floored trough with steep sides, which gives the valley its U-shape.
Examples: Glendalough and Glenmalure, Co. Wicklow.
Diagram: cross-sections of a V-shaped valley beside a U-shaped valley, with truncated spurs labelled.
1. A smaller tributary glacier joins the larger glacier that is filling the main valley.
2. Because the tributary glacier is smaller, it erodes less deeply, so its valley is left hanging above the main valley floor.
3. When the ice melts, the tributary stream falls over the edge of the hanging valley as a waterfall.
Example: Poulanass Waterfall, falling from a hanging valley into the Glendalough valley, Co. Wicklow.
Diagram: long profile of a hanging valley and its waterfall above the main valley floor.

notes.h: Ribbon lakes, paternoster lakes and fjords (erosion)
points: 1. Plucking and abrasion overdeepen a section of the valley floor more than the rest, leaving a rock basin.
2. When the ice melts, the basin fills with water, forming a long, narrow ribbon lake.
Example: Upper Lake, Glendalough, Co. Wicklow.
Paternoster lakes: a chain of rock-basin lakes along a valley floor, separated by bars of harder rock.
Tarns, ribbon lakes and kettle lakes are all glacial lakes.
3. A glacier overdeepens a coastal valley so that its floor lies well below sea level.
4. When the ice melts, the sea floods the valley, leaving a fjord with steep sides.
Examples: Killary Harbour, on the Co. Galway-Co. Mayo border; Sognefjord, Norway.
Diagram: long profile of an overdeepened valley with a ribbon lake; plan view of a fjord with steep sides and the sea at its mouth.
1. Ice flows over a bedrock outcrop, and abrasion smooths and polishes its upstream (stoss) side.
2. On the downstream (lee) side, plucking tears blocks from the rock, leaving a steep, rough face.
3. The result is a rounded hill with a smooth stoss side and a rough lee side.
Example: Lembert Dome, Yosemite, California, USA.
Striations: fine parallel scratches cut into bedrock by rock fragments held in the base of the ice; they are carved by the ice and show the direction of ice flow.
Diagram: cross-section of a roche moutonnee showing the stoss side, lee side and direction of ice flow; plan view of striations on bedrock.
Supraglacial load: debris resting on the surface of the glacier, such as rock falling from the valley sides.
Englacial load: debris trapped within the ice.
Subglacial load: debris dragged along the base; it is the most abrasive part of the load and does most of the erosion.
Glacial load is angular and unsorted: ice does not sort it by size, and it is not rounded by water as river load is.
Till (boulder clay) is unsorted and unstratified, angular material ranging from clay to boulders, deposited directly by ice.
Boulder clay plains of the Irish Midlands are formed where till is left across the land.
Deranged drainage: no clear pattern, with many lakes and marshes, forms on poorly drained glacial deposits such as till.
Lateral moraine: a ridge of till along the side of a glacier, built from debris falling from the valley walls.
Medial moraine: formed where two glaciers join, as their lateral moraines merge and run down the middle of the combined ice.
Terminal (end) moraine: an arc-shaped ridge of till at the snout, marking the furthest advance or a long pause in retreat.
Recessional moraine: a ridge of till built at the snout during a pause while the glacier retreats.
Ground moraine: a sheet of till left on the bed as the glacier melts back.
Southern Irish End Moraine: marks the southern limit of the Midlandian ice sheet.
Diagram: cross-section of a valley glacier with lateral, medial and terminal moraines labelled; plan view of an arc-shaped terminal moraine.
1. Ice deposits or overrides an accumulation of till on the bed, building an irregular mass of material.
2. Ice flowing over the mass moulds it into an elongated, streamlined hill lying parallel to the direction of ice flow.
3. The blunt, steep end faces up-ice, and the tapered end points down-ice.
4. Drumlins occur in swarms, all aligned in one direction, forming a basket of eggs landscape.
5. Where the sea floods low ground, drumlins become islands, forming drowned drumlins, as in Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.
Example: the drumlin belt across Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim.
Diagram: plan view of a drumlin swarm with an ice-flow arrow; side profile showing the blunt up-ice end and tapered down-ice end.
Erratic: a boulder carried by ice and dropped far from its source, with a rock type unlike the bedrock beneath it.
Example: granite erratics from Connemara resting on the limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare.

notes.b: Fluvio-glacial material is laid down by meltwater rather than directly by ice, so it differs from till.
points: Meltwater sorts material by size, so fluvio-glacial deposits are sorted, and layers are stratified; till is neither.
Exam classification, glacial erosion: corrie, arete, pyramidal peak, U-shaped valley, hanging valley, ribbon lake, fjord, roche moutonnee, striations.
Exam classification, glacial deposition: till, moraines, drumlins, erratics.
Exam classification, fluvio-glacial: eskers, outwash plains, kames, kettle holes.
1. Meltwater flows in a tunnel within or beneath the glacier.
2. The stream deposits sorted sand and gravel on the tunnel floor as its velocity falls.
3. When the ice melts, the deposit is left as a long, winding ridge called an esker.
Example: Esker Riada, a series of eskers across the Midlands from roughly Dublin to Galway, used as an ancient routeway (the Slí Mhór); Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, is built beside it.
Diagram: plan view of a winding esker ridge; cross-section of a ridge of sorted gravel.
1. Meltwater spreads sand and gravel beyond the terminal moraine onto flat ground.
2. The deposit forms a flat, sorted outwash plain.
Example: The Curragh, Co. Kildare, a plain of sand and gravel; it is well-drained grassland used for horse training and an army camp.
Diagram: plan view of an outwash plain lying beyond a terminal moraine.
1. Meltwater deposits sand and gravel in a hollow on the ice surface or at its margin.
2. When the ice melts, the deposit is left as a mound called a kame; where it lies against a valley side it forms a kame terrace.
3. A block of ice buried in outwash melts, leaving a hollow called a kettle hole.
Diagram: cross-section of a kame beside a kettle hole.

keyTerms.definition: Granular snow that has survived a summer and is compacted on the way to becoming glacier ice.
The upper part of a glacier where ice and snow are gained by more than they are lost.
The lower part of a glacier, including the snout, where ice is lost by melting.
The boundary between the accumulation and ablation zones, where gain and loss of ice are equal.
Movement of a whole glacier over its bed, lubricated by meltwater at the base.
Glacial erosion in which meltwater freezes in rock joints and the moving ice tears out blocks of rock.
Glacial erosion in which rock fragments frozen into the base of the ice scrape and polish the bedrock.
Fine powder ground from bedrock by glacial abrasion.
A bowl-shaped hollow on a mountainside, with a steep back wall and a rock lip, where a glacier forms.
A lake that fills a corrie after the ice has melted, held back by the rock lip.
A thin, sharp ridge left between two corries that have cut back from opposite sides.
A sharp summit left when three or more corries erode back around it, also called a horn.
A broad, flat-floored valley with steep sides, widened and deepened by a glacier from a river valley.
A blunt, cliff-like end of a valley spur cut off by a glacier filling the valley.
A tributary valley left above the floor of a main glacial valley, from which its stream falls as a waterfall.
Erosion of a section of valley floor more deeply than the rest, leaving a rock basin.
A long, narrow lake filling an overdeepened basin in a glacial valley floor.
A chain of rock-basin lakes along a valley floor, separated by bars of harder rock.
A glaciated coastal valley with steep sides and a floor below sea level, flooded by the sea after the ice melts.
A rounded rock outcrop with a smooth stoss side, formed by abrasion, and a rough lee side, formed by plucking.
Fine parallel scratches cut into bedrock by stones carried in the base of the ice, showing the direction of ice flow.
Unsorted, unstratified, angular material deposited directly by ice, ranging from clay to boulders.
A boulder carried by ice and dropped far from its source, with a rock type unlike the bedrock beneath it.
A ridge of till along the side of a glacier, built from debris falling from the valley walls.
A ridge of debris running down the middle of a glacier, formed where two glaciers join.
An arc-shaped ridge of till deposited at the snout, marking the furthest advance or a long pause in retreat.
An elongated, streamlined hill of till moulded by moving ice, with its blunt end facing up-ice.
A drumlin partly submerged when the sea floods low ground, forming an island.
A long, winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel left by a meltwater stream that flowed in a tunnel in or beneath the ice.
A flat sheet of sorted sand and gravel spread by meltwater beyond the terminal moraine.
A mound of sorted sand and gravel deposited by meltwater in a hollow on or at the edge of the ice.
A hollow left where a buried block of ice melts out of outwash.

factCards.term: Ireland's two glacial cold stages: names and extent of the ice
factCards.definition: The older Munsterian ice covered almost all of the island. The more recent Midlandian ice did not cover the far south; the Southern Irish End Moraine marks its southern limit. The Midlandian glaciation ended about 10,000 years ago.

factCards.term: Glacier snout: what makes it advance or retreat
factCards.definition: It advances when more ice arrives from the accumulation zone than melts, e.g. after heavier snowfall or cooler summers. It retreats when melting exceeds the ice arriving, e.g. with less snowfall or warmer summers, even though the ice still flows forward.

factCards.term: Skill: how to work out the average rate of snout movement
factCards.definition: Average rate = distance moved ÷ number of years, given in metres per year. Illustrative example with invented figures: a snout that retreats 600 m over 20 years moves 600 ÷ 20 = 30 m per year.

factCards.term: Corrie and tarn: how they form, in stages
factCards.definition: First, nivation and freeze-thaw enlarge a snow-filled mountain hollow; then the snow turns to ice and the rotating glacier plucks and abrades the back wall and floor, leaving a steep back wall and rock lip; finally, meltwater held behind the lip forms a tarn.

factCards.term: Name examples of corries, pyramidal peaks and an arête
factCards.definition: Corries: Coumshingaun, Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford; the Devil's Punchbowl, Mangerton, Co. Kerry. Pyramidal peaks: Carrauntoohil, Macgillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry; the Matterhorn. Arête: Striding Edge, Helvellyn, Lake District, England.

factCards.term: U-shaped valley: how it forms from a river valley, with an example
factCards.definition: A river first cuts a V-shaped valley with interlocking spurs. A glacier then deepens and widens it by plucking and abrasion and cuts off the spurs as truncated spurs, leaving a steep-sided, flat-floored trough, e.g. Glendalough and Glenmalure, Co. Wicklow.

factCards.term: Hanging valley and waterfall: how they form, with an example
factCards.definition: A tributary glacier is smaller than the main one and erodes less deeply, so when the ice melts its valley is left high above the main valley floor and its stream falls over the edge as a waterfall, e.g. Poulanass Waterfall, Glendalough, Co. Wicklow.

factCards.term: Ribbon lake: how it forms, with an Irish example
factCards.definition: Plucking and abrasion overdeepen one section of a glacial valley floor more than the rest, leaving a rock basin; when the ice melts, the basin fills with water as a long, narrow lake, e.g. the Upper Lake, Glendalough, Co. Wicklow.

factCards.term: Fjord: how it forms, with an Irish and a foreign example
factCards.definition: A glacier overdeepens a coastal valley so that its floor lies well below sea level; when the ice melts, the sea floods the valley, leaving a steep-sided inlet, e.g. Killary Harbour on the Co. Galway–Co. Mayo border, and Sognefjord, Norway.

factCards.term: Roche moutonnée: how each side forms, with an example
factCards.definition: Ice flows over a bedrock outcrop: abrasion smooths and polishes the upstream (stoss) side, while plucking tears blocks from the downstream (lee) side, leaving a steep, rough face. Example: Lembert Dome, Yosemite, California, USA.

factCards.term: Drumlin: how it forms, in stages
factCards.definition: First, ice deposits or overrides a mass of till on its bed; then the moving ice moulds it into a streamlined hill parallel to the ice flow, with a blunt up-ice end and a tapered down-ice end; drumlins lie in aligned swarms, a basket of eggs landscape.

factCards.term: Name an Irish drumlin belt and two places with drowned drumlins
factCards.definition: The drumlin belt across Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim. Drowned drumlins, islands formed where the sea flooded the low ground between drumlins: Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.

factCards.term: Esker: how it forms, with an Irish example
factCards.definition: Meltwater flowing in a tunnel within or beneath the glacier deposits sorted sand and gravel on the tunnel floor as its velocity falls; when the ice melts, a long, winding ridge is left, e.g. Esker Riada across the Midlands, the ancient Slí Mhór routeway.

factCards.term: Outwash plain: how it forms, with an Irish example and its uses
factCards.definition: Meltwater spreads sorted sand and gravel beyond the terminal moraine onto flat ground, building a flat plain. Example: the Curragh, Co. Kildare, well-drained grassland used for horse training and an army camp.

factCards.term: Glacial till vs fluvio-glacial deposits: how they differ
factCards.definition: Till is dropped directly by ice, so it is unsorted, unstratified and angular, ranging from clay to boulders. Fluvio-glacial material is laid down by meltwater, which sorts it by size and lays it in stratified layers.

factCards.term: Classify glacial landforms as erosion, deposition or fluvio-glacial
factCards.definition: Glacial erosion: corrie, arête, pyramidal peak, U-shaped valley, hanging valley, ribbon lake, fjord, roche moutonnée, striations. Glacial deposition: till, moraines, drumlins, erratics. Fluvio-glacial: eskers, outwash plains, kames, kettle holes.

factCards.term: Name an Irish example of glacial erratics
factCards.definition: Granite erratics carried by ice from Connemara rest on the limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare; their rock type is unlike the bedrock beneath them.

questions.prompt: Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram, the formation of one landform of glacial erosion.
questions.model: Corrie (cirque). Stage 1: snow collects in a hollow on the mountainside, and nivation (erosion by snow patches) and freeze-thaw weathering enlarge the hollow. Stage 2: the snow is compacted into firn and then glacier ice, which begins to move within the hollow, so the rotating ice starts to pluck and abrade the back wall and floor. Stage 3: plucking tears loose blocks of rock where meltwater has frozen in the joints, while abrasion by fragments in the ice base scrapes and polishes the surface. Stage 4: the hollow deepens and its back wall steepens, leaving a bowl with a steep back wall. Stage 5: the interior is eroded more deeply than the lower edge, which is left as a rock lip, called the threshold. Stage 6: when the ice melts, water collects in the bowl behind the rock lip and forms a tarn. Stage 7: repeated freeze-thaw and mass movement keep the back wall steep. Example: Coumshingaun, Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford, and the Devil's Punchbowl, Mangerton, Co. Kerry. Diagram: a plan view of a bowl-shaped hollow with the steep back wall labelled; a cross-section showing the steep back wall, the rock lip and the tarn, with an arrow for the rotational movement of the ice and a label for the accumulation zone above it.

questions.prompt: Examine the formation of one landform of glacial deposition or fluvio-glacial deposition.
questions.model: Drumlin. Ice deposits or overrides an accumulation of till on the bed, building an irregular mass of unsorted material. As the ice keeps flowing over the mass, it moulds the material into an elongated, streamlined hill lying parallel to the direction of ice flow. The blunt, steep end faces up-ice, where the ice came from, and the tapered end points down-ice. Drumlins occur in swarms, all aligned in one direction, which records the direction of former ice flow. Where the sea floods low ground, drumlins become islands, forming drowned drumlins, as in Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down. Example: the drumlin belt across Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim. Diagram: a plan view of a drumlin swarm with an ice-flow arrow, and a side profile showing the blunt up-ice end and the tapered down-ice end.

questions.prompt: Name and explain the formation of two landforms of glacial erosion.
questions.model: U-shaped valley. Before glaciation the valley is V-shaped, cut by a river. A glacier fills the valley and deepens and widens its floor by plucking and abrasion. The glacier cuts off the river's interlocking spurs, leaving blunt truncated spurs. The result is a broad, flat-floored trough with steep sides, which gives the valley its U-shape. Example: Glendalough and Glenmalure, Co. Wicklow. Diagram: cross-sections of a V-shaped valley beside a U-shaped valley, with truncated spurs labelled. Pyramidal peak. Three or more corries erode back around one summit from different directions. Their back walls retreat, so the summit is left as a sharp, pointed peak called a horn. Example: Carrauntoohil, Macgillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry, Ireland's highest mountain. Diagram: a plan view of a horn ringed by three corries.
